overview: The Angevin Empire was the collection of lands brought together under Henry II and his family, including England, Normandy, Anjou and Aquitaine. Inheritance, marriage and political expansion joined these territories under related rulers. Family rivalries and conflict with the French monarchy eventually broke apart much of this cross-Channel dominion.

periods.title: A cross-Channel dynasty takes shape
periods.summary: Henry became king of England in 1154 after acquiring Normandy and Anjou and marrying Eleanor of Aquitaine. His authority linked territories with different histories, rather than creating them all at once.

periods.title: Royal justice reaches local communities
periods.summary: The Assize of Clarendon set out procedures for sworn accusations, sheriffs’ custody and hearings before royal justices. Local testimony became part of a coordinated system of criminal investigation.

periods.title: Revolt within the ruling family
periods.summary: Eleanor supported her sons’ revolt against Henry. After its failure she was held in custody, including at Old Sarum. The struggle shows how dynastic relationships could threaten the structure of royal power.

periods.title: Building at Dover
periods.summary: Henry began a major rebuilding of Dover Castle in the 1180s. Its great tower combined security, royal accommodation and ceremonial display near the crossing used by pilgrims to Canterbury.

periods.title: Richard’s reign and Eleanor’s authority
periods.summary: Richard released Eleanor when he succeeded Henry in 1189. She returned to political activity during a reign in which Richard spent much of his time away on crusade and elsewhere.

periods.title: John inherits contested dominions
periods.summary: Richard’s death brought John to the throne. Conflict with the French king put the continental lands under mounting pressure, leading to major territorial losses.

periods.title: Normandy is lost
periods.summary: Château-Gaillard fell on March 6, 1204, and mainland Normandy passed to the French king that year. The Channel Islands were an exception. The conquest sharply reduced John’s continental position.

periods.title: A charter fails to secure peace
periods.summary: The agreement made at Runnymede in June 1215 was soon annulled by the pope, and civil war followed. Magna Carta’s later influence depended on subsequent reissues, not uninterrupted acceptance of the first settlement.

sections.title: Discovering village work at Wharram Percy

items.text: At Wharram Percy in Yorkshire, excavators found postholes and beam slots beneath later houses. These traces indicate timber-built dwellings before the thirteenth century. They preserve evidence of ordinary construction even where the wood has disappeared, and help distinguish earlier households from the stone buildings visible in later phases.

Excavation beside the village stream revealed successive low clay dams and a millpond for a horizontal water mill. This system began before Angevin rule and remained in use into the thirteenth century. Its successive alterations show a community maintaining water-powered grain processing over generations.

sections.title: Castles as architecture and statements of power

items.text: Dover’s great tower had a long approach through a forebuilding, with stairs reaching the second floor before descending into a hall. Its paired hall-and-chamber arrangement and conspicuous exterior suited grand receptions. Historians interpret these features as evidence for ceremony and hospitality as well as defense.

The tower was built without fireplaces and used hearths and braziers for heat. English Heritage links its elaborate rebuilding to high-ranking visitors traveling to Becket’s shrine. That connection is a historical interpretation from architecture and events; the modern furnished rooms are reconstructions of a possible royal interior.

Richard’s Château-Gaillard was constructed above the Seine between 1196 and 1198 to help protect the river route and Rouen. Its position and defensive design show the importance of controlling approaches through Normandy. The stronghold’s capture in 1204 also demonstrates that an imposing fortress could be overcome.

sections.title: Craft, devotion and connections across the Channel

items.text: A Limoges reliquary now in the British Museum is made of gilded copper alloy with champlevé enamel and is dated to about 1210 in the exhibition catalogue. It depicts Becket’s murder near an altar and his ascent to heaven. Its materials and imagery connect specialized metalwork with the expanding cult of an English saint.

The catalogue compares the reliquary with a similar example in the Louvre. Differences in Becket’s posture show makers adapting a shared religious subject. These are devotional images made after the killing, not eyewitness pictures. The British Museum object’s known collecting history does not establish its original medieval owner.

sections.title: Records, legal practice and ordinary obligations

items.text: The surviving English pipe rolls become a nearly continuous series from 1155, although an earlier roll covers 1129 to 1130. Their survival gives historians an unusually long sequence of royal financial records. The start of the continuous series under Henry II should not be mistaken for the invention of royal accounting.

The 1166 Assize of Clarendon required sworn reports from twelve men of a hundred and four from each village about suspected serious offenders. Accusation could lead to the ordeal of water. This was a procedure for presenting suspects, with forms of proof very different from a modern criminal jury trial.

The same text required sheriffs to coordinate with justices, instructed counties without jails to build them, and ordered written lists of fugitives. These provisions show government depending on messengers, buildings, timber and clerical work. They describe official requirements, not proof that enforcement was identical in every county.

Eleanor of Aquitaine’s inheritance was central to the dynasty’s continental position, and she continued to exercise political authority. Her long captivity after the revolt and her renewed activity under Richard reveal both the reach of a queen’s power and its vulnerability within the royal family.

Magna Carta addressed baronial rights, property and practical grievances against the king. Its provisions concerning lawful judgment and access to justice later acquired broader meanings. The 1215 settlement did not establish equal rights for everyone, and its immediate failure to end conflict belongs alongside its enduring reputation.

Later rulers reissued the charter after John’s death. The U.S. National Archives displays a 1297 version that was entered into England’s statute rolls. Distinguishing that surviving document from the 1215 agreement shows how an institutional legacy could be reshaped long after the Angevin territorial union weakened.

ending.text: The Angevin dominions broke apart through warfare and dynastic conflict. John lost Normandy and Anjou to the French monarchy, while the Plantagenet dynasty continued to rule England. This was a loss of territorial power, not the disappearance of the populations and institutions of those lands. The map’s 1279 endpoint does not date a single imperial fall.
